strengths: Strong theoretical contributions: O(log(1/ϵ)) oracle complexity for hypergradient approximation (improvement from O(ϵ⁻¹)) and Õ(δ⁻¹ϵ⁻³) bilevel convergence matching state-of-the-art nonsmooth nonconvex optimization

Elegant active-set reduction technique (Theorem 4.5) that converts general constrained problems to equality-constrained surrogates while preserving hypergradient accuracy—this is the key conceptual innovation
Solver-agnostic design enabling use of advanced solvers (GUROBI, MOSEK) without solver-specific differentiation, with practical implementation as PyTorch layer
Comprehensive experimental validation showing significant memory and runtime advantages for ill-conditioned problems; superior memory scaling (Figure 6) compared to KKT-based methods
Detailed ablation studies (Appendix G.2) including gradient accuracy validation (Figure 11 showing >0.9 cosine similarity), solver tolerance sensitivity, and batch size effects
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (especially Figure 1 for ghost problem) and well-structured proofs
weaknesses: Strong active-set identification assumption (4.3) is fundamental limitation: Appendix F.1 proves no continuous estimator works without it; alternative (Theorem F.2) requires smoothing with additional log factor; limited guidance on detecting when assumption fails in practice

Restrictive assumptions for general convex constraints (Assumption D.1): requires oracle sharing same active constraints (circular requirement), additional technical bounds (D.1.3), and counterexample (Eq. 30) shows value function may be non-Lipschitz—these significantly limit 'general convex constraints' claim

Finite-difference approximation error O(δ) accumulates across iterations; setting δ in practice underdiscussed; experiments use fixed tolerances but global error propagation through training not thoroughly analyzed

Limited experimental scope: largest scale dy=800; primarily synthetic/decision-focused learning tasks; Sudoku is somewhat artificial; real applications (control, meta-learning) not demonstrated; Alt-Diff baseline excluded; CPU-only evaluation
Incremental novelty: builds heavily on Kornowski et al. (2024) framework; active-set reduction is main new component; bilevel reformulation and finite-difference approximation are existing techniques
Code reproducibility issue: source code URL appears blank in manuscript; hyperparameter specifications for baselines incomplete; some experimental details relegated to appendices

strengths: Addresses important practical bottleneck in differentiable optimization with novel active-set reduction approach
Solid theoretical contributions: O(log(1/ε)) complexity for hypergradient approximation improves over O(ε^-1) penalty methods
Rigorous theoretical analysis with convergence guarantees O˜(δ^-1 ε^-3) matching best-known rates for nonsmooth optimization
Well-engineered practical implementation: solver-agnostic library, drop-in replacement for CvxpyLayer
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple baselines and ablation studies demonstrating memory efficiency
Creative technical approach combining bilevel reformulation, active-set linearization, and finite-differences
weaknesses: Critical Assumption 4.3 (active-set identification) is strong and unvalidated in practice—no empirical analysis of when constraints transition between active/inactive states during optimization, and theory shows without this assumption the problem becomes intractable
Limited to synthetic/toy problems (dy≤1000); no real-world decision-focused learning, control, or meta-learning applications tested despite claims of broad applicability
Computes approximate hypergradients with O(δ) error vs. exact methods; cumulative approximation error over training iterations and downstream optimization impact never analyzed

Strong assumptions limit scope: requires lower-level strong convexity (Assumption 4.2) and extension to general convex constraints (Assumption D.1) introduces many additional technical assumptions that significantly weaken claimed generality
Baseline comparisons raise fairness concerns: LPGD requires non-default tolerance (10^-12 vs 10^-4), and method uses CPU-only solvers despite solver-agnostic claims

Overstated claims: method is not 'fully first-order' (still solves two optimization problems per backward), not truly 'solver-agnostic' (requires problem-specific gradient construction and linearization), and not a true 'drop-in replacement' (requires restructuring lower-level formulation)
No empirical validation of active-set identification correctness in experiments; Figure 11 shows gradient similarity but doesn't confirm active-set property holds

Missing key ablations and analysis: no comparison of active-set reduction alone vs. simple finite-differences, no sensitivity analysis for constraint transitions, no degradation analysis when assumptions violated

Theoretical constants in O˜(δ^-1 ε^-3) bound potentially dimension-dependent with unanalyzed hidden constants; no discussion of how strong convexity parameter µ_g or condition numbers affect practical performance

strengths: Novel active-set reduction technique that elegantly converts inequality-constrained bilevel problems to equality-constrained surrogates, enabling O(log(1/ε)) oracle complexity
Strong theoretical contributions: Theorem 4.6 and Corollary 4.7 match best-known rates for nonconvex nonsmooth optimization with meaningful improvement over penalty-based methods
Solver-agnostic design via clever surrogate objective reformulation (Eq. 6) enables integration with state-of-the-art solvers (GUROBI, MOSEK) without solver-specific differentiation
Comprehensive experimental validation showing comparable convergence to exact methods with significant speedup on ill-conditioned problems and sublinear memory/time scaling
Well-written paper with clear motivation, intuitive illustrations (Figure 1), detailed proofs in appendices, and open-source implementation
weaknesses: Assumption 4.3 (active-set identification) is critical but largely unverified empirically; no checks in experiments validate that active sets are actually identified correctly; Appendix F shows this assumption is necessary (Lemma F.1), limiting practical applicability
Theory requires exact solutions to Problems P0 and P3, but experiments use approximate solutions; gap between theory and practice for solution accuracy not thoroughly analyzed

Restricted scope: limited to convex lower-level problems excluding meta-learning with neural networks; general convex constraints require additional assumptions (Assumption D.1) that essentially outsource the main difficulty

Limited experimental validation: only synthetic tasks (DFL, Sudoku, SOCP) without real-world applications; moderate problem sizes (dy ≤ 1000); no comparison with implicit differentiation on well-conditioned problems where KKT methods excel
Perturbation parameter δ selection not well-discussed; practical guidance for choosing δ given ε unclear; constants hidden in O(log(1/ε)) notation not made explicit
Assumption 4.2 requires lower-level strong convexity, which is restrictive; LICQ constraint qualification not checked empirically; no discussion of violations or relaxations in practice
